name: lens
intent: Focus on one part of an immutable structure through a composable getter/setter pair, so a nested field can be read and replaced without hand-writing the copy chain or repeating the path at every call site.
problem: Updating one nested field of immutable data means hand-writing the copy cascade at every level (`p.copy(home = p.home.copy(city = ...))`, `{ ...p, home: { ...p.home, city } }`): the path is duplicated at every call site, a schema change ripples through all of them, and the intent "this is the same field" cannot be stored, passed or composed.
context: Immutable, product-shaped domain data nested several levels deep - records, case classes, data classes, plain maps - where the same nested field is viewed and replaced from many places, where an update path is data (configurable, passed to helpers, derived from a schema) rather than fixed code, and where the language or a library already provides a copy-with primitive to build the new value from. Typical in functional-style domain models, undo/snapshot and optimistic-UI state, AST/compiler transformations and test-data builders.
benefits: The update path is written once as a value: the same focus can be stored, passed to helpers, composed with other foci and reused at every call site instead of being re-derived as a hand-written copy cascade.
Composition: two single-field lenses compose into one deeper lens, so access at depth N is built from N definitions and the whole path stays type-checked end to end.

The data stays immutable, so old and new versions are both valid values - which is what makes undo, snapshots, sharing between threads and structural sharing of unchanged subtrees possible - while callers keep assignment-like ergonomics (set/modify).
Schema changes localise: the field definition and its lens change in one commit, and call sites that compose the lens keep working.
The getter/setter contract is checkable independently of the data flow: the lens laws (set-get, get-set, last-set-wins, purity) are testable as properties of the optic itself.
tradeoffs: The laws are not enforced anywhere: an improper lens (a setter that normalises, clamps, reorders or drops unrelated structure) composes silently into updates that disagree with direct reads, and no compiler diagnoses it.

Every update pays an extra layer: a copy at each level of the focus plus, in library or van-Laarhoven encodings, closures and wrapper values per composed focus - measurably slower than a direct copy-and-assign and visible in hot loops.

Debugging gets more indirect: stack traces and error messages point at optic internals rather than the business field, and functor/profunctor encodings have a real learning curve for a team new to them.

Copying is shallow by default, so structural sharing means nested mutable children stay aliased between the old and the new value - a correctness trap wherever the immutability discipline is not enforced deeply.
Adoption cost: hand-written withers, the language's own copy-with construct and library optics are not interchangeable, so introducing a lens library ripples through call sites and dependencies.
Over-abstraction: for a single fixed path in one function, the two-line copy the lens replaces is shorter, dependency-free and easier to read.

participants.responsibility: Bundles the two operations for one focus and composes with other lenses (Lens[S,A] and Lens[A,B] yield Lens[S,B]); it is a value, not a utility method on the data type.
The immutable structure the lens is applied to; it is never changed - an update produces a new whole and leaves the original valid.
The single part of the whole the lens exposes: one field, a list index, a map key, one position of a tuple.
Pure function Whole -> Focus that reads the focus and changes nothing (the purity part of the lens contract).
Pure function (Whole, Focus) -> Whole' that returns a copy of the whole with only the focus replaced, preserving every other part (get-set and last-set-wins).
Binds an outer lens to an inner lens so the outer focus becomes the inner whole, and is the carrier of "paths as values".

use_cases: Configuration, feature-flag and rule documents nested several levels deep that many components patch by path.
Undo/redo, snapshots and optimistic UI or game state, where every version must stay a valid value and updates must be structural rather than in place.
Compilers, ASTs and code generators: rewrite one node deep in a tree while the rest of the tree stays shared.
API/DTO round-tripping: apply a partial change to a decoded immutable payload without re-building the whole model by hand.
Test data builders and fixtures: a base fixture plus focused overrides expressed as composed lenses.
Cross-module access layers where several features reference the same deep path and a duplicated path would drift out of sync.
GraphQL selective-field updates: a client sends a partial mutation payload and the server applies exactly the focused fields using composed lenses, leaving unmentioned fields untouched.
React component state (useState/setState) or Redux immutable state: a focused lens on a deep slice avoids spreading the entire top-level state object at every update.

YAML/TOML configuration files parsed into immutable objects: configuration services that need to patch one deep key (e.g., a feature flag) derive a lens from the schema rather than re-serialising the whole config.
Deep patch operations in HTTP PATCH APIs: the JSON pointer path maps directly to a composed lens, so the update is applied structurally rather than by string-manipulating the JSON.

Event-sourced aggregate state replay: lens paths are stored as event metadata so that the aggregate root can be partially reconstructed or patched at a known path without replaying the entire event log.
Property-based test data generation: a base fixture plus focused overrides expressed as composed lenses let the same fixture serve many test cases without deep copying.

Haskell applications that use Edward Kmett's Control.Lens package for immutable domain and game state: compose Lens and Traversal values to read, replace or modify nested records without repeating copy cascades.
Scala case-class domain models using Monocle's GenLens and Focus APIs: compose address and street lenses, then get, replace or modify deeply nested immutable fields.
TypeScript immutable object updates using optics-ts: compose an author/name lens and use compiler-checked get, set or modify operations for nested state.
avoid_when: One fixed path is updated once or twice: the language's own copy-with construct (record `with`, case-class `copy`, `dataclasses.replace`, spread, struct update syntax) is shorter and needs no dependency.
The model is mutable by design - in-place updates, caches, large arrays mutated for throughput: a lens adds indirection to work the language already does directly.
The focus may be absent or repeated (optional field, list element, map lookup): that is an Optional/Traversal, and a total lens over it throws or fabricates a value.
The structure is not a product but a sum type/variant: focusing into one case needs a Prism; using a lens there produces a partial setter.
The codebase only ever updates one level and the team has no functional background: the laws, encodings and dependency cost more than the duplication they remove.
anti_patterns: "Lens everything": wrapping every field in an optic in a language whose records/case classes already generate accessors and a copy-with construct, so access becomes indirection with nothing reused.
Improper lenses used as normalisers: setters that clamp, trim or reformat the focused value, so get-set/set-get fail and composed updates silently disagree with direct reads.
A total lens over a genuinely optional field or a list, producing exceptions or fabricated defaults where an Optional/Traversal is required.
Setters that mutate in place "for speed": the copy discipline is then a lie and previously handed-out versions change under their holders.
Maintaining the same path twice - once as a lens and once as hand-written copy code - so the two drift apart at the next schema change.
design_principles: Separation of access from structure: the focus is described independently of the code that reads or writes it.
Purity and referential transparency: get and set are pure functions, so property tests on the laws replace defensive copying.
Composition over inheritance: complex access is built by composing simple foci, not by adding accessor methods to the data types.
Single source of truth for a path: a nested location is defined once and reused everywhere it is updated.
Information hiding: callers depend on the focus, not on the concrete nesting of the representation.
best_practices: Define each lens next to the type it focuses on, so a schema change updates the optic in the same commit as the field.
Property-test the three laws (set-get, get-set, last-set-wins) for every hand-written lens; derive generated lenses instead of typing them.
Prefer the language's copy-with construct or a maintained optics library, and hand-write a lens only when the same focus is genuinely reused or passed around.
Model absent or repeated foci as Optional/Traversal (and variant foci as Prism) instead of loosening a lens's totality.
Keep setters structurally faithful: replace the focus, leave everything else identical - no normalisation, no reordering, no default filling.
Decide and document the sharing boundary - which levels are deep-copied and which are shared - wherever the value crosses a thread, cache or persistence edge.
Use Iso for structurally isomorphic types (e.g., newtype wrappers, bidirectional converters) before reaching for Lens — an Iso costs nothing at runtime and documents the intent.

Prefer generated or derived optics (case-class derives in Scala/Monocle, @optics in Haskell, derive in TypeScript) over hand-written ones: generated optics are correct by construction and survive schema changes.
Property-test the three lens laws (set-get, get-set, last-set-wins) as part of the unit test suite for every hand-written lens; do not assume composition preserves the laws.

Keep optics values internal to a module and expose only the Lens type alias or an opaque setter function in public APIs, so the internal encoding (Van Laarhoven vs profunctor) remains an implementation detail.

When combining optics with JSON handling (e.g., Aeson in Haskell, optics-ts with Aeson in TypeScript, serde in Rust), prefer a library with native optics integration so the focus path and the JSON path stay in sync automatically.
Limit composed-lens depth: a lens deeper than 4–5 levels generates many intermediate objects on every update; consider a Zipper or a flat model with embedded values instead.
Document the totality contract explicitly: a total Lens must never fail on the focus; if the focus can be absent use Optional/Traversal and document that set throws on empty.

In multithreaded code, verify structural-sharing guarantees at each level of the value: which levels are deep-copied and which are shared must be explicit wherever the value crosses a thread or cache boundary.
sources: Foster, Greenwald, Moore, Pierce & Schmitt, "Combinators for Bi-directional Tree Transformations: A Linguistic Approach to the View-Update Problem" (POPL 2005) - the origin of lenses as well-behaved bidirectional transformations: https://doi.org/10.1145/1047659.1040325
